activities.anchor: crash analysis, rocketry and particle physics
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the law nature refuses to bend
activities.name: mcLedgerCloze

config.text: Momentum is mass times velocity, p = mv. Newton's original second law says force is the %%0%% of change of momentum, and when two objects collide their momentum changes are equal and %%1%% — so the system's total never drifts.
config.hint: F = Δp/Δt, plus the third law acting for exactly the same instant.

activities.anchor: not a violation of conservation but its tidiest exhibit
activities.caption: find the faulty line — signs are the whole method
activities.name: mcSignSpot

config.prompt: One line of this collision answer is wrong — click it:
lines: Two carts approach: 4 kg at +5 m/s and 6 kg at −3 m/s.
They couple, so the 10 kg wreckage carries all 2 kg·m/s: v = 2/10 = 0.2 m/s.
The 6 kg cart's momentum must have been +18, since it was moving faster.
Head-on collisions that stop dead are the case where the momenta exactly cancel.
config.correction: The 6 kg cart moving at −3 m/s carries −18 kg·m/s — without the sign, the ledger is meaningless.
config.why: Momentum is a vector: pick a positive direction and keep it. 'Moving faster' says nothing without a sign — the +20 − 18 arithmetic only works because the signs were kept.

activities.caption: bet first — the club and the ball
activities.name: mcGolfPredict

config.q: A golf club head (heavy) strikes a golf ball (light) in an elastic collision. Compared with the club head's speed, the ball leaves…
choices: slower — the club shares its momentum with the ball
at nearly double the club head's speed
config.why: The heavy-strikes-light elastic limit launches the light object at nearly twice the incoming speed — the same reason a Newton's cradle's end ball exits at the incoming speed.

activities.caption: true or false — the two currencies
activities.name: mcCurrencyJudge

statements.s: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system.
statements.why: Exact, always — even when the wreckage crumples.

statements.s: Kinetic energy is conserved when the carts stick together.
statements.why: 36 J became 9 J in the worked case — three quarters went into crumpling, heating and sound.

statements.s: The lost kinetic energy is destroyed.
statements.why: It changed currency — thermal and acoustic energy, which the thermodynamics chapter tracks.

statements.s: Solving a collision usually starts with deciding which quantity is conserved.
statements.why: Momentum always balances; kinetic energy only in the elastic special case.

activities.anchor: momentum conservation with nothing to brace against
activities.caption: rebuild the skater's recoil, step by step
activities.name: mcSkaterOrder

config.prompt: A 60 kg skater at rest throws a 3 kg ball forward at 10 m/s. Order the bookkeeping:
items: Before: total momentum is zero — skater and ball both still
The ball leaves carrying 3 × 10 = 30 kg·m/s forward
The skater must carry 30 kg·m/s backward
The centre of mass never moved
config.why: An explosion is a collision in reverse: momenta sum to zero, kinetic energy goes UP (paid for by the muscle's chemistry), and the ledger stays exact in both directions.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the hero's real recoil
activities.name: mcHeroEstimate

config.prompt: A 10 g bullet at 400 m/s embeds in an 80 kg hero. Roughly what recoil speed does momentum actually give them?
config.why: Bullet momentum: 0.01 × 400 = 4 kg·m/s. Shared over 80 kg: 0.05 m/s — a nudge, not a flight.
config.context: Films show ten metres of backward flight; conservation allows five centimetres per second.

activities.anchor: answered by the momentum ledger, not by the damage
activities.caption: pair each question with the physics that answers it
activities.name: mcToolMatch

pairs.right: scales with speed squared — you're spending kinetic energy

pairs.left: harder to stop: a 30,000 kg truck at 1 m/s or a 100 kg cyclist at 30 m/s?
which vehicle changed velocity more in the crash?
pairs.right: equal third-law forces, different masses — ask the ledger

pairs.left: why the hero flies backward from a pistol shot

config.why: Momentum answers 'how hard to stop'; kinetic energy answers 'what braking costs'; both beat the damage report.

activities.anchor: the wave's speed must be wavelength divided by period
activities.caption: fill the blanks — same fork, two media
activities.name: wsForkCloze

config.text: A tuning fork vibrates at 440 Hz (concert A) and sound leaves it at 343 m/s, so the wavelength in air is λ = v/f ≈ %%0%% m. Dip the fork in water and strike steel instead: the same 440 Hz vibration would launch a wave about %%1%% m long — same frequency, different %%2%%, different wavelength.
config.hint: λ = v/f; the speed in steel is about 5,900 m/s. What survives the boundary is the frequency.

activities.anchor: where water genuinely does move shoreward
activities.caption: bet first — the ball after the ripples
activities.name: wsBallPredict

config.q: Ripples cross a pond, passing a floating ball. Once the ripples have gone, where is the ball?
choices: Swept several metres toward the shore, carried by the wave
Exactly where it was — it bobbed in little circles
Pushed to the bottom by the wave's pressure
config.why: What travels is the pattern and its energy; the medium's particles oscillate about fixed positions. (Surfers are the exception that proves the rule — they ride the breaking part, where water truly moves.)

activities.anchor: so the two sounds annihilate before reaching your eardrum
activities.caption: pair the behaviour with its everyday exhibit
activities.name: wsBehavioursMatch

config.prompt: Four behaviours cover nearly everything a wave can do — match them to their exhibits:

pairs.right: the straight straw that looks bent in water
hearing someone around the corner but not seeing them

config.why: Sound and light obey the same four — and the headphone trick is interference in real time: the ambient noise played back half a cycle out of phase.

activities.anchor: raises the pitch by one octave
activities.caption: rebuild the 12th-fret sequence
activities.name: wsFretOrder

config.prompt: From open string to octave — put the standing-wave logic in order:
items: An open string, pinned at both ends, only sustains waves whose wavelength fits
Nodes are forced at each pinned end
Pressing at the 12th fret halves the vibrating length
The frequency doubles — one octave up
config.why: Standing waves demand nodes where the string is pinned; v = f·λ turns half the length into double the frequency.

activities.caption: place the speed of sound on the scale
activities.name: wsSpeedPlace

config.prompt: Sound's speed is the medium's decision. Place its speed in air at 20 °C (m/s):
config.why: 343 m/s in cool air — and stiffness beats density: water carries it at 1,480, steel at 5,900, diamond at 12,000.
config.context: The rule of thumb: stiff, light media carry sound fast; dense-but-squishy media carry it slowly.

activities.anchor: resolve millimetre-scale structures in a fetus
activities.caption: call the magnitude — middle C's wavelength
activities.name: wsMiddleCEstimate

config.prompt: Middle C vibrates at 262 Hz, and sound runs at 343 m/s. Roughly what wavelength does it launch in air?
config.why: λ = v/f = 343/262 ≈ 1.3 m — arm's length again.
config.context: The piano's top note, 4,186 Hz, manages just 8 cm — pitch up, wavelength down.

activities.anchor: forgetting it is the classic exam error
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the echo arithmetic
activities.name: wsEchoSpot

config.prompt: One line of this echo answer is wrong — click it:
lines: You shout at a cliff and hear the echo 1.2 s later; sound runs at 343 m/s.
The sound made a round trip: to the cliff and back.
So the distance is d = v·t/2 = 343 × 1.2 / 2 ≈ 206 m.
Sonar skips the factor of 2, since the seabed return is one-way only.
config.correction: Sonar keeps the factor of 2 — the ping travels down AND back, so 1,480 × 2.0 / 2 = 1,480 m.
config.why: Every echo is a round trip. The submarine's ping goes down and comes back exactly like the shout; dropping the 2 is the classic exam error.

activities.anchor: the same phenomenon at different frequencies
activities.caption: file the family — longer, visible, or shorter
activities.name: wsFamilyBuckets

config.prompt: One continuous family, one narrow visible band. File each member:

items.label: FM radio at 100 MHz — a 3 m wave
Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz — a 12.5 cm wave

config.why: Radio, microwave and infrared all run longer than visible; ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays run shorter — an FM station and a dental X-ray are the same phenomenon at different frequencies.
